","char_count":825,"fact_ids":[],"source_anchors":[]},{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":3,"domain":"Illinois impaired driving","heading":"C — impaired driving","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Illinois impaired driving

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol affects sight and slows reactions, and even a small amount can raise crash risk before the legal intoxication threshold is reached. [A01]
Why it matters: group Alcohol effects; recall cue Impairment can begin below legal threshold.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
Blood-alcohol concentration measures alcohol through testing of breath, blood, urine or another bodily substance. [A01]
Why it matters: group Alcohol concentration; recall cue Concentration comes from bodily-substance testing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
Driving at a blood-alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent or higher is illegal, and impairment can support a driving-under-the-influence conviction below that level. [A01]
Why it matters: group Alcohol concentration; recall cue Threshold does not make lower impairment lawful.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
Food recently eaten, tolerance and other drugs can affect a person’s response to alcohol. [A01]
Why it matters: group Alcohol effects; recall cue Alcohol response has several factors.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A01
Only time removes alcohol’s effects; food, coffee and showers do not accelerate its elimination. [A01]
Why it matters: group Alcohol effects; recall cue Coffee does not sober a driver.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A01
The handbook prohibits highway driving with cannabis concentration at least five nanograms per milliliter of whole blood or ten nanograms per milliliter of another bodily substance. [A01]
Why it matters: group Drug impairment; recall cue Cannabis threshold depends on tested substance.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A01
Medical or recreational cannabis use does not permit driving while impaired. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue Authorized cannabis does not authorize impaired driving.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A01
The handbook requires vehicle-transported cannabis to be in a sealed container resistant to odor and access by children. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue Cannabis transport has container conditions.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A01
Neither the driver nor a passenger may use cannabis inside a motor vehicle. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue No cannabis consumption in vehicle.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A01
When an officer reasonably suspects cannabis impairment during a stop, the driver must submit to field-sobriety testing, validated roadside chemical testing or both. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue Reasonable suspicion can require cannabis testing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A01
Refusing the stated cannabis tests or failing field-sobriety or validated roadside chemical testing leads to license suspension under the handbook’s rule. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue Cannabis testing refusal or failure affects license.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A01
Cannabis-impaired driving or unlawful vehicle transportation can lead to loss of driving privileges and a two-year medical-cannabis card revocation for a registered patient. [A01]
Why it matters: group Cannabis rules; recall cue Cannabis offense can affect driving and patient card.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A02
Many prescribed and nonprescription medicines can impair driving, including allergy, cold and pain remedies. [A02]
Why it matters: group Drug impairment; recall cue Legal medicine may still impair driving.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A02
Combining even a little alcohol with other drugs is dangerous. [A02]
Why it matters: group Drug impairment; recall cue Alcohol and drugs can be dangerous together.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0052]
","char_count":4053,"fact_ids":["sec09-F01","sec09-F02","sec09-F03","sec09-F04","sec09-F05","sec09-F06","sec09-F07","sec09-F08","sec09-F09","sec09-F10","sec09-F11","sec09-F12","sec09-F13","sec09-F14"],"source_anchors":[{"anchor_id":"A01","source_page":"src:rdmv-il-d:illinois-secretary-of-state-driver-servi:handbook:pdf-0051"},{"anchor_id":"A02","source_page":"src:rdmv-il-d:illinois-secretary-of-state-driver-servi:handbook:pdf-0052"}]},{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.02","merge_seq":4,"domain":"Illinois impaired driving","heading":"C — impaired driving","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Illinois impaired driving

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A01
An Illinois driving-under-the-influence conviction remains permanently on the driving record, and arrest or conviction can result in lost driving privileges, registration consequences, fines or imprisonment. [A01]
Why it matters: group DUI consequences; recall cue DUI has enduring record consequences.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A01
Driving on Illinois roads gives implied consent to specified alcohol or drug tests using breath, blood, urine or another bodily substance. [A01]
Why it matters: group Implied consent; recall cue Road use carries implied testing consent.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A01
Following a crash causing injury or death, police with probable cause of impairment must request alcohol or drug testing. [A01]
Why it matters: group Implied consent; recall cue Serious crash and probable cause require test request.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A01
A driver may arrange additional tests by a qualified person of the driver’s choosing at the driver’s own expense. [A01]
Why it matters: group Implied consent; recall cue Additional chosen testing is self-funded.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A01
A person convicted of impaired driving may owe up to five hundred dollars for blood-test costs after breath-test refusal or an officer’s belief that blood testing could reveal drugs. [A01]
Why it matters: group Implied consent; recall cue Blood-test expense has stated circumstances.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A01
A chemical test meeting the listed alcohol or cannabis thresholds results in a six-month summary suspension, as does detection of the specified substances from unlawful use. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Failed chemical test brings summary suspension.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A01
Refusing chemical testing ordinarily results in a one-year suspension. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Chemical-test refusal has longer ordinary suspension.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A01
A qualifying summary action, out-of-state test-refusal suspension, impaired-driving supervision or impaired-driving conviction within five years makes the driver a second offender for the listed summary penalties. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Recent qualifying history changes summary penalty.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A01
For a second offender under the stated five-year rule, chemical-test refusal causes a three-year suspension and a failed chemical test causes a one-year suspension. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Repeat refusal differs from repeat failure.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A01
Refusal to take a chemical test may be used as evidence against the driver. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Refusal can become evidence.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A01
At arrest the officer takes the license and, if it is valid, issues a temporary receipt allowing forty-five days of driving; summary suspension starts on the forty-sixth day after notice. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Temporary receipt ends before suspension begins.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A01
A summary suspension does not terminate until the reinstatement fee is paid and the driving record is updated. [A01]
Why it matters: group Summary suspension; recall cue Elapsed time alone does not end suspension.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A02
Refusing chemical testing after involvement in a crash with serious injury or death brings a revocation of at least one year. [A02]
Why it matters: group Summary revocation; recall cue Serious-crash refusal has revocation consequence.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A01
A driving-under-the-influence conviction can be imposed in addition to a statutory summary suspension or revocation. [A01]
Why it matters: group Conviction penalties; recall cue Administrative action and conviction can coexist.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A01
The general conviction table lists revocation minimums of one year for a first conviction, five years for a second within twenty years and ten years for a third. [A01]
Why it matters: group Conviction penalties; recall cue General revocation minimums increase with convictions.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A01
A fourth or later driving-under-the-influence conviction results in lifetime revocation. [A01]
Why it matters: group Conviction penalties; recall cue Fourth conviction has lifetime consequence.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A01
A concentration of zero point one six percent or more, or transporting a child younger than sixteen during impaired driving, can bring enhanced punishment. [A01]
Why it matters: group Conviction penalties; recall cue High concentration or young passenger can enhance penalties.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A01
Restoring privileges after impaired-driving revocation can require substance-use evaluation, rehabilitation or education, an administrative hearing, a reinstatement fee and other conditions. [A01]
Why it matters: group Restoration; recall cue Restoration requires more than waiting.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A01
A driving-under-the-influence conviction requires financial-responsibility insurance to be filed for three years. [A01]
Why it matters: group Restoration; recall cue DUI conviction requires insurance filing.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A01
An Illinois resident’s out-of-state impaired-driving conviction or test refusal is reported to Illinois, recorded and treated administratively as a comparable Illinois offense. [A01]
Why it matters: group Out-of-state offenses; recall cue Out-of-state DUI history reaches Illinois.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A01
An eligible first-time offender may seek a Monitoring Device Driving Permit requiring an approved breath-alcohol ignition interlock installation for driving relief during summary suspension. [A01]
Why it matters: group Ignition interlock; recall cue Driving relief requires approved interlock.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A01
Unless found indigent, the offender pays the monitoring-permit, interlock-installation and monitoring costs. [A01]
Why it matters: group Ignition interlock; recall cue Interlock relief generally has offender-paid costs.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A01
The agency monitors the interlock during the permit and receives alerts about attempts to start after drinking or to tamper with the device. [A01]
Why it matters: group Ignition interlock; recall cue Interlock reports alcohol attempts and tampering.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A01
A first-time offender may decline monitoring relief and refrain from driving, but driving during that suspension without participating in the program is a felony. [A01]
Why it matters: group Ignition interlock; recall cue Declining permit means refraining from driving.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A02
Impaired driving can be aggravated when it involves a crash with injury or death, is a third or later offense or follows a qualifying history of reckless homicide or a fatal aggravated offense. [A02]
Why it matters: group Aggravated offenses; recall cue Serious consequences and history can aggravate DUI.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R13 | anchor: A02
Impaired driving can be aggravated when committed with children on a school bus, while operating a for-hire vehicle or without the required license, permit or insurance. [A02]
Why it matters: group Aggravated offenses; recall cue Vehicle use and missing qualifications can aggravate DUI.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R14 | anchor: A01
Alcohol consumption in a vehicle is generally illegal for drivers and passengers, with the handbook’s exception for passengers on nonschool charter buses, motor homes, mini motor homes and limousines. [A01]
Why it matters: group Open containers; recall cue Passenger exemptions are limited to listed vehicles.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R15 | anchor: A01
An opened alcoholic-beverage container may not be kept in the passenger compartment. [A01]
Why it matters: group Open containers; recall cue Open alcohol stays out of passenger area.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R16 | anchor: A01
Operating a motorboat under alcohol, drug or intoxicating-compound impairment is illegal, and an injury or fatal boating crash can also lead to driving-privilege loss for refusal or specified failed testing. [A01]
Why it matters: group Motorboats; recall cue Impaired boating can affect road privileges.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R17 | anchor: A01
A parent or guardian may not allow under-twenty-one drinking or fail to control access to alcohol on controlled property, including vehicles or watercraft, and resulting injury or death can bring criminal punishment. [A01]
Why it matters: group Providing alcohol; recall cue Controlled property includes vehicles and boats.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec09-R18 | anchor: A02
Driving while suspended or revoked for the listed impaired-driving, reckless-homicide or serious hit-and-run offenses can bring jail, a longer withdrawal period and seizure or forfeiture of the vehicle. [A02]
Why it matters: group Suspended driving; recall cue Driving during serious withdrawal adds consequences.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R19 | anchor: A02
An Illinois suspension or revocation for the listed serious offenses prohibits driving in every state, and an out-of-state arrest for violating it is reported to Illinois. [A02]
Why it matters: group Suspended driving; recall cue Illinois withdrawal follows driver across state lines.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R20 | anchor: A02
Do not knowingly allow an impaired person to drive your vehicle. [A02]
Why it matters: group Providing alcohol; recall cue Do not lend vehicle to known impaired driver.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R21 | anchor: A02
Conviction for supplying alcohol to someone younger than twenty-one may result in a fine, jail and license suspension. [A02]
Why it matters: group Providing alcohol; recall cue Supplying underage alcohol can affect license.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R22 | anchor: A02
For a driver younger than twenty-one, a first impaired-driving conviction brings at least two years of revocation. [A02]
Why it matters: group Young-driver alcohol rules; recall cue Young first DUI has longer minimum.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R23 | anchor: A02
A driver younger than twenty-one with any alcohol trace while operating a vehicle faces at least a three-month suspension. [A02]
Why it matters: group Young-driver alcohol rules; recall cue Young-driver alcohol rule reaches any trace.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R24 | anchor: A02
Under-twenty-one conviction or supervision for illegal alcohol consumption, purchase, possession or receipt as a gift causes driving-privilege loss even when the person was not driving. [A02]
Why it matters: group Young-driver alcohol rules; recall cue Underage alcohol offense can affect nondriver privileges.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R25 | anchor: A02
A suspension occurring before age twenty-one requires successful remedial driver education and can require the full license examination before reissuance. [A02]
Why it matters: group Young-driver alcohol rules; recall cue Young suspension requires remedial education.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec09-R26 | anchor: A02
The handbook warns that impaired-driving laws change continually and directs readers to the agency’s current impaired-driving fact book or website. [A02]
Why it matters: group Currency; recall cue DUI provisions require current issuer review.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]
